status: drafted via multi-agent workflow, adversarially fact-checked and corrected
notes: Mark is the shortest and fastest-paced Gospel — heavy on action and miracle-narrative, light on extended discourse (three real teaching blocks: the parables of ch. 4, the defilement teaching of ch. 7:14-23, and the Olivet Discourse of ch. 13, versus Matthew's five major discourses). This produced a roster weighted toward vivid single-scene miracle recipients (Jairus, the woman with the issue of blood, the Gerasene demoniac, the Syrophenician woman, Bartimaeus) each getting a full tier, since Mark gives these scenes unusually specific, personally-embodied detail compared to their parallels in the other Gospels. Two Passion-narrative figures originally filed as jesus_mark submanagers were promoted to full manager tiers on review: the centurion at the cross, whose "Truly this man was the Son of God" is the book's climactic human confession at the moment of death, and Joseph of Arimathaea, who personally goes in boldly to Pilate and personally prepares and entombs the body — under this file's own rule-3 test (would removing them change the scene's outcome?), both plainly do. Per the established Gospel rule, Jesus gets his own fully independent tier (id jesus_mark, NOT shared with Matthew's "jesus") — themed "The Opened Heavens" after 1:10 ("he saw the heavens opened") at his baptism, which deliberately echoes 15:38 ("the veil of the temple was rent in twain") at his death, a real structural bracket unique to how Mark frames the book. Simon Peter anchors the remaining ten apostles as submanagers (ancient tradition, reflected in Papias's account preserved by Eusebius, holds Mark's own Gospel derives from Peter's preaching — noted as tradition, not asserted as textual fact since Mark's own text never claims Petrine authorship); Mark's own ordination list at 3:16-19 orders them Simon, James, John, Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Canaanite, Judas — Andrew is fourth in Mark's own text, not second (that ordinal belongs to Matthew's own apostle list, and has been corrected here to avoid importing it). James and John (the "sons of thunder") are kept as one combined submanager entry for the scenes where Mark's text pairs them without individual distinction, but Mark 9:38-41 — where John alone speaks and acts, independent of James — is included in that entry's verse list rather than silently dropped, so the entry doesn't overstate how consistently the pair is undifferentiated. Levi/Matthew's dual naming (2:14 vs. 3:18) is flagged as a traditional identification, not something Mark's own text explicitly states. Two deliberate accuracy calls: (1) Mark's trial narrative (14:53-15:1) never actually names the high priest — unlike Matthew 26:3/57, which does name Caiaphas — so this file keeps him as "The High Priest" (id high_priest_mark) with a flag noting John 18:13 and Matthew both identify him as Caiaphas by cross-reference, rather than importing that name into a text that doesn't use it. (2) Mark 16:9-20 (the appearances, Great Commission, and ascension) is included but flagged as the "Longer Ending" — absent from the earliest and best Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus), a well-established textual-critical fact rather than doctrinal commentary; the book's actual, earliest-attested text ends abruptly at 16:8 ("neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid"), which is itself flagged as a distinct Mark-specific narrative beat. The man of great possessions (10:17-22) is deliberately NOT called "young" or a "ruler" here, since Mark's own text calls him only "one" — those descriptors belong to Matthew 19:20 and Luke 18:18 respectively and are not imported. Naming collisions are unusually dense in this book: FIVE different men named Simon appear and are all indexed distinctly (Simon Peter, Simon the Canaanite/apostle, Simon the leper of Bethany 14:3 — whose house hosts the alabaster-box anointing, now given his own minor character entry rather than only being mentioned inside another entry's verse note — Simon of Cyrene 15:21, and Simon the brother of Jesus 6:3); TWO Marys beyond Jesus's own mother (Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses); a real risk of conflating Herodias's unnamed dancing daughter (6:22, never named in Mark — extra-biblical tradition via Josephus calls her Salome) with Salome the disciple who is independently and by-name present at the cross and tomb (15:40, 16:1) — these are two different women who happen to share a name only in secondary tradition, flagged explicitly on both entries. Jesus's brothers (James, Joses, Juda, Simon — 6:3) also share names with several of the Twelve without being the same people; kept out of the main character list as a genealogyLists bulk reference with the collision flagged rather than risk silent conflation. The messianic secret (Jesus repeatedly commanding silence after miracles/exorcisms — 1:25, 1:34, 1:44, 3:12, 5:43, 7:36, 8:30, 9:9) is a recurring motif rather than a single event, so it's captured as a funFact on Jesus's own entry instead of forced into a tier of its own. A third law-type tier, "That Which Defileth" (7:14-23), was added on review alongside the ch. 4 parables and ch. 13 Olivet Discourse — Jesus's teaching that defilement comes from within a man rather than from external ritual failure, delivered as the direct positive counterpart to the preceding confrontation with the Pharisees and scribes over the tradition of the elders (7:1-13). The book now totals 19 scribe tiers (16 person-type, 3 law-type).

genealogyLists.note: Bulk or deliberately-unresolved references, kept out of the character list above.

twelveApostlesList.note: The full ordination list of the Twelve, given together in one place, in this order: Simon (Peter), James and John (sons of Zebedee, Boanerges), Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James (son of Alphaeus), Thaddaeus, Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot.

jesusBrethren.note: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us?" Named as Jesus's brothers: James, Joses, Juda(s), and Simon, plus unnamed sisters. NAMING COLLISION FLAG: this James and this Simon share names with two of the Twelve (James son of Alphaeus/James son of Zebedee, Simon the Canaanite/Simon Peter), and this Juda(s) shares a name with Judas Iscariot — none of these are the same people as their namesake apostles; the text gives no basis for merging them, so they are kept out of the indexed character list entirely rather than risk a false identification.

manyOtherWomen.note: Beyond Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome, the text notes "many other women which came up with him unto Jerusalem" followed and ministered to him in Galilee — an unindividuated collective, not differentiated by name.

longerEndingTextualNote.note: Widely recognized by textual scholars as absent from the earliest and most reliable Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus); some manuscripts instead carry a much shorter alternate ending. This is a textual-transmission fact, not a doctrinal judgment about the content's truth — flagged here purely so the game's content doesn't present 16:9-20 as having the same manuscript certainty as 1:1-16:8.

characters.name: Jesus Christ

verses.note: Opening line: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God."
Baptized by John; heavens opened, Spirit descends as a dove, voice declares "Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."
Driven into the wilderness, tempted of Satan forty days, with the wild beasts, angels minister to him.
Begins preaching in Galilee after John's imprisonment: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand."
Stills the storm on the Sea of Galilee: "Peace, be still."
Rejected at his home town, Nazareth: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" Marvels at their unbelief.
Feeds the five thousand with five loaves and two fishes.
Walks on the sea; calms the disciples' fear: "It is I; be not afraid."
Feeds the four thousand.
At Caesarea Philippi asks "Whom say ye that I am?"; Peter answers "Thou art the Christ."
First prediction of his death and resurrection; rebukes Peter, "Get thee behind me, Satan."
Transfigured before Peter, James, and John; Moses and Elias appear and talk with him; voice from the cloud: "This is my beloved Son: hear him."
Second Passion prediction.
Third, most detailed Passion prediction on the road to Jerusalem.
Triumphal entry into Jerusalem on a colt.
Curses a barren fig tree; it withers, used to teach on faith and prayer.
Cleanses the temple, overturning the tables of the moneychangers.
Institutes the Lord's Supper at the Passover meal.
Prays in Gethsemane, "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt."
Darkness over the land; cries "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"; gives up the ghost.
The veil of the temple is rent in twain from the top to the bottom at his death — the deliberate structural echo of the heavens 'opened' at his baptism (1:10).
The young man at the tomb declares: "He is risen; he is not here."

The 'Longer Ending' — appearances to Mary Magdalene and others, the Great Commission ("Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature"), the ascension. Textually absent from the earliest and best Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus); included here but flagged as a known textual-critical issue, not part of Mark's earliest-attested text, which ends at 16:8.

funFacts: The 'messianic secret' — Jesus repeatedly commands silence after healings/exorcisms and even from his own disciples about his identity (1:25, 1:34, 1:44, 3:12, 5:43, 7:36, 8:30, 9:9) — is one of Mark's most distinctive recurring motifs, more pronounced here than in any other Gospel.
Mark contains no birth narrative or genealogy at all — it opens directly with John the Baptist's ministry, unlike Matthew and Luke.
6:3 calls him 'the carpenter' directly (not just 'the carpenter's son' as in Matthew 13:55) — the only Gospel to do so.

characters.name: Mary, mother of Jesus

verses.note: She and Jesus's brethren come seeking him; he asks "Who is my mother, or my brethren?" and points to those who do the will of God.
Referred to as "the son of Mary" by the townspeople of Nazareth — the only place in Mark she is named.

funFacts: Mark never narrates a virgin birth or any nativity account — her role in this Gospel is limited to these two brief mentions.

characters.name: John the Baptist

verses.note: Preaches the baptism of repentance in the wilderness; all Judaea and Jerusalem go out to him.
Clothed with camel's hair and a leathern girdle about his loins; eats locusts and wild honey.
"There cometh one mightier than I after me... I have baptized you with water: but he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost."
Baptizes Jesus in the Jordan.
"Now after that John was put in prison, Jesus came into Galilee."
Herod had bound him in prison for Herodias' sake; John had told Herod, "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife."
Herod feared John, knowing him a just and holy man, kept him safe, and heard him gladly.
Beheaded at Herod's birthday feast at the request of Herodias' daughter; his head brought in a charger.
His disciples take up his corpse and lay it in a tomb.

funFacts: Mark 6:14-16 records that Herod, on hearing of Jesus's works, feared John had risen from the dead — the rumor that frames the whole flashback account of his death.

characters.name: Simon Peter

spouses: peter's wife — unnamed, implied only by his mother-in-law at Mark 1:30, not individually indexed

verses.note: Called by Jesus while casting a net into the sea with Andrew; "I will make you to become fishers of men"; they forsake their nets.
Named among the Twelve; Jesus surnames him Peter.
At Caesarea Philippi: "Thou art the Christ."
Rebukes Jesus over the Passion prediction and is himself rebuked: "Get thee behind me, Satan."
Present at the Transfiguration; offers to build three tabernacles, "not knowing what to say; for they were sore afraid."
Vows he will not deny Jesus even if all others do; told he will deny him thrice before the cock crow twice.
Found asleep in Gethsemane: "Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?"
Follows afar off into the high priest's palace; denies Jesus three times; the cock crows the second time; he remembers Jesus's word and weeps.
The young man at the empty tomb singles him out by name: "go your way, tell his disciples and Peter that he goeth before you into Galilee."

funFacts: Church tradition (Papias, via Eusebius) holds that Mark's own Gospel preserves Peter's preaching — noted as tradition; Mark's own text makes no such claim about its source.

verses.note: Simon's brother; called together with him while casting their net.

Listed fourth among the Twelve, after Simon, James, and John — Mark's own ordering differs from Matthew's apostle list, where Andrew appears second; corrected here to avoid importing that ordinal from the wrong Gospel.
One of the four (with Peter, James, John) who ask Jesus privately about the destruction of the temple, prompting the Olivet Discourse.

characters.name: James and John, sons of Zebedee (Boanerges)
characters.perkNote: Kept as one combined entry for most scenes, where Mark's text pairs them together without differentiating (the calling, the Boanerges naming, the Transfiguration, the request to sit at Jesus's right and left hand, Gethsemane) — but Mark 9:38-41 is a real exception where John alone speaks and acts, independent of James, and is included below rather than omitted, so this entry doesn't overstate how consistently the pair is undifferentiated.

genealogy.mother: salome_disciple_mark — traditional identification via comparison with Matthew 27:56, not stated by Mark itself; flagged, not asserted

verses.note: Called from mending their nets in the ship with their father Zebedee; leave him and follow Jesus.
Surnamed Boanerges, "the sons of thunder."
Present with Peter at the Transfiguration.

John alone (not James) says, "Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us." Jesus answers, "Forbid him not... for he that is not against us is on our part," followed by the teaching that even a cup of water given in his name will not lose its reward.
Ask to sit on Jesus's right and left hand in his glory; told "ye know not what ye ask"; the other ten are moved with indignation against them.
Taken with Peter further into Gethsemane.

funFacts: The identification of their mother as Salome rests on comparing Mark 15:40/16:1 with Matthew 27:56, not on anything Mark itself states directly — flagged as a cross-Gospel inference, not settled fact.
Mark 9:38-41 is the one scene in this book where John acts and speaks independently of his brother James, despite the pair otherwise being treated as a unit throughout.

verses.note: Listed among the Twelve; Mark gives no individual action for him beyond this.
Listed among the Twelve; Mark gives no individual action for him beyond this.

characters.name: Levi (Matthew) the publican
characters.perkNote: Mark calls him 'Levi the son of Alphaeus' at his calling (2:14) but lists 'Matthew' among the Twelve (3:18); tradition holds these are the same tax-collector figure (paralleling Matthew 9:9, which uses the name 'Matthew' for this same calling story), but Mark's own text never explicitly states the two are one person — flagged as an inference, not asserted here as settled fact, the same discipline applied elsewhere in this file to the Salome and 'James the less' identifications.

genealogy.father: alphaeus — Mark 2:14, shared name with James son of Alphaeus (3:18); not stated whether the same Alphaeus, not asserted either way

verses.note: Called by Jesus while sitting at the receipt of custom; "Follow me. And he arose and followed him."
Jesus eats in his house with publicans and sinners; "They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick."
Listed among the Twelve as "Matthew."
Listed among the Twelve; Mark gives no individual action for him beyond this.

characters.name: James, son of Alphaeus
characters.perkNote: Naming collision: a different James from James son of Zebedee (of 'sons of thunder'). Sometimes traditionally identified with 'James the less' of 15:40, but Mark itself never makes this identification explicit — flagged, not asserted.

genealogy.father: alphaeus — Mark 3:18, shared name with Levi's father (2:14); same man or not is not stated by the text

verses.note: Listed among the Twelve; Mark gives no individual action for him beyond this.
Listed among the Twelve; Mark gives no individual action for him beyond this.

characters.name: Simon the Canaanite
characters.perkNote: One of five different men named Simon in Mark (Simon Peter, Simon the Canaanite, Simon the leper of 14:3, Simon of Cyrene of 15:21, and Simon the brother of Jesus of 6:3) — all kept distinct, never merged.

verses.note: Listed among the Twelve as "Simon the Canaanite"; Mark gives no individual action for him beyond this.
Lay sick of a fever in Simon's house; Jesus takes her by the hand and lifts her up; the fever leaves her and "she ministered unto them."

characters.name: The Parables of the Kingdom
characters.purpose: Teaches, through agricultural imagery familiar to a Galilean audience, how the kingdom of God is received, hidden, and grows — the sower explains why the same message produces different results in different hearers; the candle teaches that what is hidden is meant to come to light; the seed growing secretly and the mustard seed both teach that the kingdom's growth is God's own quiet, inevitable work, not something forced by human effort.

verses.note: Parable of the sower — seed on the wayside, stony ground, among thorns, and on good ground.
Jesus privately explains the sower to the disciples.
Parable of the candle: "Is a candle brought to be put under a bushel?"
Parable of the seed growing secretly — unique to Mark among the Synoptics.
Parable of the mustard seed, "less than all the seeds that be in the earth," which grows greater than all herbs.
Jesus taught in parables publicly "as they were able to hear it" but explained all things privately to his own disciples.

characters.name: The Gerasene Demoniac ("Legion")

verses.note: A man with an unclean spirit lives among the tombs, cannot be bound even with chains, cries and cuts himself with stones day and night.
"My name is Legion: for we are many"; begs not to be sent out of the country.
The spirits enter a herd of about two thousand swine, which run violently down a steep place into the sea and are drowned.
Found sitting, clothed, and in his right mind.
Begs to go with Jesus but is told instead to go home and publish what great things the Lord has done for him — a rare instance where Jesus commands proclamation rather than silence.

funFacts: The region is given as "the country of the Gadarenes" in the KJV text (5:1); the exact place-name varies across manuscripts and Gospel parallels, a known textual variation.

verses.note: A ruler of the synagogue, falls at Jesus's feet, besought him greatly for his daughter who "lieth at the point of death."
Told his daughter is dead; Jesus says "Be not afraid, only believe."
Weeping and wailing found at his house; Jesus puts the mourners out.
Jesus takes the child by the hand: "Talitha cumi... Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." She rises and walks; he commands she be given something to eat, and that no man know it.

characters.name: Jairus's Daughter

verses.note: Raised from apparent death by Jesus.

funFacts: Her stated age ("twelve years old," 5:42) is one of the very few precise ages given anywhere in Mark.

characters.name: The Woman with the Issue of Blood

verses.note: Had an issue of blood twelve years, suffered many things of many physicians, spent all that she had, was nothing bettered but grew worse.
Comes in the press behind Jesus and touches his garment, saying within herself, "If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole."
Immediately her fountain of blood dries up; she feels in her body that she is healed.
Jesus, perceiving virtue had gone out of him, asks who touched him; she comes fearing and trembling and tells him the whole truth.
"Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague."

characters.name: Herod Antipas
characters.perkNote: Mark calls him "king Herod" (6:14), though historically he ruled only as tetrarch — a known imprecision in the text itself, not an error introduced here. Distinct from Herod the Great (Matthew 2) and Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12), neither of whom appear in Mark.

verses.note: Hears of Jesus's fame; fears John, whom he beheaded, has risen from the dead.
Had bound John in prison for Herodias' sake, his brother Philip's wife, whom he had married.
Herodias holds a grudge against John; Herod himself feared John, knowing him a just and holy man, kept him safe, and heard him gladly.
On his birthday makes a supper for his lords; the daughter of Herodias dances and pleases him; he swears to give her up to half his kingdom.
"The king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath's sake, and for their sakes which sat with him, he would not reject her."
Sends an executioner, who brings John's head in a charger.
Formerly the wife of Herod's brother Philip; Herod married her.
"Therefore Herodias had a quarrel against him, and would have killed him; but she could not."
When her daughter asks what to request, she instructs her: "The head of John the Baptist."

characters.name: Herodias's Daughter
characters.perkNote: Never named in Mark's own text. Later Jewish tradition (via Josephus, not scripture) calls her Salome — not asserted here as fact. Explicitly NOT the same person as Salome the disciple who is present at the cross and tomb (15:40, 16:1); those two figures are only linked by a shared traditional name, never by the biblical text itself.

verses.note: Comes in and dances, pleasing Herod and his guests.
Goes out and asks her mother what she should request, then comes in and asks for John's head in a charger "by and by."
Receives the head and gives it to her mother.

characters.name: That Which Defileth
characters.purpose: Delivered first to the multitude and then explained privately to the disciples, this teaching relocates true defilement away from external ritual failure (eating with unwashed hands, the disputed tradition of the elders in 7:1-13) to the internal condition of the heart — nothing entering a man from without can defile him, but the evil thoughts and deeds that proceed out of a man from within do. It functions as Jesus's positive teaching answer to the Pharisees' and scribes' preceding accusation.

verses.note: Calls the multitude to him: "There is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him: but the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man."

Entering into a house away from the people, the disciples ask him concerning the parable; he explains that whatsoever entereth in at the mouth cannot defile since it enters not the heart but the belly, and goes out into the draught, purging all meats.

"That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man. For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lasciviousness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness: All these evil things come from within, and defile the man."

funFacts: Mark's own narrative aside at 7:19 ("This he said, making all meats clean") is the Gospel writer's own editorial comment on the teaching's implication, not words spoken by Jesus himself within the quoted teaching.

children: her daughter — Mark 7:25-30, not individually indexed, had an unclean spirit and is healed at a distance

verses.note: A Greek, a Syrophenician by nation, falls at Jesus's feet in the borders of Tyre and Sidon, beseeching him to cast a devil out of her daughter.

Jesus: "Let the children first be filled: for it is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it unto the dogs." She answers: "Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs."
"For this saying go thy way; the devil is gone out of thy daughter." She goes home and finds the devil gone out, and her daughter laid upon the bed.
Named specifically as "blind Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus," sits by the highway begging near Jericho — unusually specific naming for a healed person in Mark.
Cries out, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me"; many charge him to hold his peace, but he cries the more.
Casts away his garment, rises, and comes to Jesus.
"Thy faith hath made thee whole." He immediately receives his sight, and follows Jesus in the way.

characters.name: The Olivet Discourse
characters.purpose: Delivered privately to four of the Twelve in response to a prediction that the temple would be utterly destroyed, this teaching prepares the disciples for coming upheaval, warns against being deceived by false christs, describes the coming persecution and "abomination of desolation," and repeatedly presses the point that no one knows the day or hour — the point is readiness and watchfulness, not calculation.

verses.note: Prediction that not one stone of the temple will be left upon another.
Peter, James, John, and Andrew ask him privately on the Mount of Olives when these things will be.
Warnings of false christs, wars and rumors of wars, earthquakes and famines — "these are the beginnings of sorrows."
Predicts persecution, being delivered up to councils and rulers; "he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved."
The "abomination of desolation," flight into the mountains, tribulation such as was not from the beginning of creation.
Sun and moon darkened, stars falling, the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory.
Parable of the fig tree: when its branch is tender and puts forth leaves, summer is near — likewise these signs mean the time is near.
"Of that day and that hour knoweth no man... Watch ye therefore."

characters.name: The Woman with the Alabaster Box
characters.perkNote: Unnamed in Mark's own text. John 12:3 identifies a woman doing a similar act as Mary of Bethany — a different Gospel's account, noted but not imported as fact into Mark's own version, since the scene details (house of Simon the leper, timing) differ somewhat between the two.

verses.note: In the house of Simon the leper at Bethany, breaks an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard, very precious, and pours it on Jesus's head.
Some at the table have indignation, saying the ointment might have been sold for above three hundred pence and given to the poor.

Jesus defends her: "She hath done what she could... Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her."

characters.name: Judas Iscariot
characters.perkNote: Naming collision: Jesus's own brother is also called "Juda" at 6:3 — a different man entirely, not indexed as a separate character here but flagged in genealogyLists.

verses.note: Listed last among the Twelve: "and Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him."
Goes to the chief priests to betray Jesus; they are glad and promise to give him money.
At supper, told one of the Twelve eating with Jesus will betray him: "good were it for that man if he had never been born."
Comes with a great multitude with swords and staves; gives a prearranged kiss-sign: "Master, master"; kisses him.

funFacts: Unlike Matthew 27:3-5, Mark's own text never records what became of Judas afterward — no remorse scene, no death, nothing beyond the betrayal and kiss.

characters.name: The High Priest
characters.perkNote: Mark's own text never names him — unlike Matthew 26:3/57, which does name Caiaphas. John 18:13 independently identifies the high priest of this year as Caiaphas. Kept unnamed here to stay faithful to what Mark's own text actually says, with the cross-Gospel identification flagged rather than imported as Mark's own claim.

verses.note: Jesus is led away to the high priest; all the chief priests, elders, and scribes assemble.
Seeks witness against Jesus to put him to death, but the testimonies do not agree.
Asks directly, "Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" Jesus answers, "I am."
Rends his clothes: "What need we any further witnesses? Ye have heard the blasphemy: what think ye?" All condemn him to be guilty of death.
The chief priests, with the elders, scribes, and the whole council, bind Jesus and deliver him to Pilate.

characters.name: The Chief Priests, Elders, and Scribes (the Council)

verses.note: Chief priests and scribes seek how they might take Jesus by craft and put him to death.
The whole council seeks witness against Jesus at his trial.
Hold a consultation in the morning and deliver Jesus to Pilate.
Move the people to ask instead for Barabbas.
Question his eating with sinners and healing on the sabbath; take counsel with the Herodians to destroy him.
Question why his disciples eat with unwashen hands, challenged over the tradition of the elders.
Seek a sign from heaven, tempting him.
Ask about the lawfulness of divorce, tempting him.
Sent with the Herodians to catch Jesus in his words over tribute to Caesar.
"Which say there is no resurrection"; pose the riddle of a woman with seven husbands to trap him; told "Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, neither the power of God."
Asks Jesus, "Art thou the King of the Jews?" Jesus answers, "Thou sayest it."
The chief priests accuse him of many things; Jesus answers nothing more, and Pilate marvels.
Offers to release a prisoner per custom of the feast; the crowd, moved by the chief priests, asks for Barabbas instead; asks "what evil hath he done?" but they cry the more, "Crucify him."
Willing to content the people, releases Barabbas, and delivers Jesus, when he had scourged him, to be crucified.
Marvels that Jesus was already dead; confirms it with the centurion before giving the body to Joseph of Arimathaea.
Lay bound with those that had made insurrection with him, who had committed murder in the insurrection.
Released instead of Jesus at the crowd's demand.

characters.name: The Centurion at the Cross
characters.perkNote: Promoted from a jesus_mark submanager to a full manager tier on review: his declaration is the book's climactic human confession of Jesus's identity, occurring at the precise moment of death — removing him removes the only explicit outsider testimony that closes the crucifixion account, a real change to the scene's outcome under this file's own rule-3 test.

verses.note: Standing over against Jesus, seeing how he cried out and gave up the ghost, declares: "Truly this man was the Son of God."
Confirms to Pilate that Jesus is already dead, before Pilate grants the body to Joseph of Arimathaea.

funFacts: Mark never names this centurion; he is identified only by his role and his position "over against" the cross.

characters.name: Joseph of Arimathaea
characters.perkNote: Promoted from a jesus_mark submanager to a full manager tier on review: he personally goes in boldly to Pilate to request the body and personally prepares and entombs it — without him Jesus's body has no burial at all in Mark's account, a real change to the scene's outcome under this file's own rule-3 test.

verses.note: An honourable counsellor, who also waited for the kingdom of God, goes in boldly unto Pilate and craves the body of Jesus.

Pilate, having confirmed Jesus is dead via the centurion, gives him the body; Joseph buys fine linen, takes him down, wraps him in the linen, and lays him in a sepulchre hewn out of a rock, then rolls a stone unto the door of the sepulchre.

characters.name: Mary Magdalene
characters.perkNote: One of at least two Marys in the book's final chapters (alongside Mary the mother of James and Joses) — kept distinct.

verses.note: Beholds the crucifixion afar off, named first among the women present.
With Mary the mother of Joses, beholds where Jesus is laid.
Buys sweet spices with the other women to come and anoint the body.
Finds the stone rolled away; a young man in white tells them Jesus is risen; they flee the sepulchre afraid and say nothing to any man — the abrupt earliest ending of Mark.
Longer Ending (textually disputed, absent from the earliest manuscripts): Jesus appears to her first, described as the one "out of whom he had cast seven devils."

characters.name: Mary, mother of James and Joses
characters.perkNote: A different Mary from both Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Jesus. Her son 'James' is sometimes traditionally equated with James son of Alphaeus (one of the Twelve), but Mark's own text never makes that identification explicit — flagged, not asserted.

children: james the less/James — Mark 15:40, not individually indexed as distinct from james_alphaeus_mark, identification uncertain

verses.note: Beholds the crucifixion afar off with Mary Magdalene and Salome.
Beholds where Jesus is laid.
Brings spices to anoint the body.

characters.name: Salome (disciple)
characters.perkNote: IMPORTANT naming caution: this Salome is independently named at the cross and tomb (15:40, 16:1). She is NOT the same person as Herodias's unnamed dancing daughter (6:22), whom only extra-biblical tradition (not scripture) also calls Salome — the two are unrelated within Mark's own text and must not be conflated.

verses.note: Beholds the crucifixion afar off with the two Marys.
Brings spices to anoint the body.

characters.name: Man with an Unclean Spirit (Capernaum synagogue)

verses.note: Jesus's first recorded miracle in Mark; the spirit cries out "art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God"; Jesus casts it out and commands it be silent.
Kneels and beseeches Jesus, "If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean"; is healed and charged to say nothing, but instead publishes it widely.

characters.name: The Paralytic and His Four Bearers

verses.note: Four men uncover the roof of the house and let down the bed on which the paralytic lies; Jesus forgives his sins and heals him, to the scribes' astonishment.

characters.name: The Man with the Withered Hand

verses.note: Healed in the synagogue on the sabbath; the Pharisees watch to accuse Jesus, then plot with the Herodians to destroy him.

characters.name: The Deaf Man with a Speech Impediment

verses.note: Healed in the region of Decapolis; Jesus says "Ephphatha, that is, Be opened"; the man's ears are opened and his tongue loosed.
Healed in two stages, unique to Mark: after the first touch he says "I see men as trees, walking"; after the second his sight is fully restored.

characters.name: The Man with Great Possessions
characters.perkNote: Mark's own text calls him only "one" who "had great possessions" (10:17, 22) — it never calls him young (that detail is from Matthew 19:20) or a ruler (that's from Luke 18:18). Kept to Mark's own wording rather than importing cross-Gospel detail, the same discipline applied elsewhere in this file (e.g. the alabaster-box woman's John 12:3 caveat).

verses.note: Runs to Jesus and kneels, asking what he must do to inherit eternal life; told to keep the commandments, then to sell what he has and give to the poor; "he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions."

characters.name: The Scribe Who Asked the Greatest Commandment

verses.note: Asks which is the first commandment of all; agrees with Jesus's answer (love God, love neighbor); told "Thou art not far from the kingdom of God."
Casts in two mites into the treasury; Jesus says she "of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living."

characters.name: The Young Man Who Fled Naked

verses.note: Follows Jesus at his arrest wearing only a linen cloth about his naked body; when seized, he leaves the cloth and flees naked — a detail unique to Mark, unexplained by the text itself.

funFacts: Some later interpreters have speculated this figure is Mark himself making a cameo appearance, but this is not stated anywhere in the text and is flagged here only as speculation, not fact.

characters.name: Simon of Cyrene
characters.perkNote: One of five different men named Simon in Mark — kept distinct from Simon Peter, Simon the Canaanite, Simon the leper, and Simon the brother of Jesus.

verses.note: A passer-by coming out of the country, father of Alexander and Rufus, compelled to bear Jesus's cross — a detail specific enough (naming his sons) to suggest his family was known to Mark's original audience.

characters.name: Simon the Leper
characters.perkNote: One of five different men named Simon in Mark (Simon Peter, Simon the Canaanite, Simon the leper of Bethany, Simon of Cyrene, and Simon the brother of Jesus of 6:3) — kept distinct from all of them; nothing else is stated about him beyond his house being the setting for the alabaster-box anointing.

verses.note: The anointing at Bethany takes place "in the house of Simon the leper" — his only appearance in the text; nothing further is said of him, including whether he was still afflicted with leprosy at the time or previously healed.
